text: Retain overlayfs, FUSE, user namespaces and seccomp-bpf in the fork and verify them from the Linux personality at V1 (Chromium sandbox, Flatpak/bubblewrap and podman depend on them).
Provide a ptrace-equivalent for the Linux personality (gdb, strace, Wine debugging, Crashpad) gated by an explicit debug capability.
Define a Steam runtime sub-corpus (pressure-vessel, gamescope, user namespaces, 32-bit multilib, /dev/input via udev, SDL game-controller evdev) with its own scenario scripts.
Decide whether ia32 (32-bit) emulation is retained in the fork before any syscall-pruning work, since Steam and many Windows titles depend on it.
Decide that X11 primary selection is emulated inside the Wayland/X11 bridge and never crosses into the native clipboard.
Decide whether the Linux personality userland is built from source or redistributes an existing distribution's binaries, and settle the resulting trademark and license obligations.
rationale: Redistributing another distribution's packages inherits its trademark rules and source-offer duties.

text: Define upstream engagement policies with freedesktop.org projects (Wayland, PipeWire, xdg portals), Mesa and systemd for the Linux personality.
rationale: Linux compatibility is a product and its components have upstreams that must not be forked casually.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Integrate Linux compatibility conformance suites (LTP, glibc tests, selected syzkaller Linux descriptions in differential mode against upstream Linux, and an application smoke corpus) into nightly CI for the Linux personality.
rationale: §56.3 says compatibility is a product, and a product needs a regression suite that measures behavioural divergence from real Linux.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Bound the Linux personality's ambient POSIX authority by the enclosing component's capability set so that a Linux process can never reach a resource its component was not granted, regardless of uid or file mode.
rationale: Compatibility inherits history (§3) but must not become the ambient-authority hole that makes the capability model meaningless in practice.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Provide compatibility shims: org.freedesktop.secrets and libsecret for Linux applications, and Windows Credential Manager/DPAPI for the Windows personality, both backed by the native secrets service with per-application scoping.
rationale: Browsers, mail clients and games store credentials through these APIs and must work without granting them a shared password store.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Provide PAM/NSS-equivalent, logind (org.freedesktop.login1) and D-Bus session-bus compatibility for Linux applications, fed from the native identity and Session services so getpwuid, $HOME, XDG_RUNTIME_DIR and session lock/idle signals behave as expected.
rationale: §56.3 says Linux compatibility is a product; desktop applications break in subtle ways without these identity and session facts.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the default capability bundle for Linux and Windows compatibility applications (which directories, network, devices) and how portal-style requests upgrade it, so legacy applications work without either ambient home access or constant prompting.
rationale: Compatibility apps have no manifest of requested capabilities, and getting this default wrong either breaks them or hollows out the security model.

text: Expose the native font store to the Linux personality through a fontconfig-compatible view and to the Windows personality through the Wine font directory so all three worlds see the same installed fonts.
rationale: Users install a font once and expect every application, native or compat, to see it.

text: Bridge the native IME to Linux apps via zwp_text_input_v3 and an IBus/Fcitx-compatible D-Bus endpoint, and to Windows apps via Wine's IMM32/TSF path, so one active IME types into every window.
rationale: Users switch between native and compat windows constantly and cannot tolerate different IME state per window class.

text: Compat notification bridges: org.freedesktop.Notifications and portal notification D-Bus for Linux apps and Windows toast/balloon APIs via Wine mapped onto the native service with per-app grants.
rationale: Compat apps must appear in the same notification center and be subject to the same do-not-disturb policy.

text: Emulate the NetworkManager D-Bus API and resolv.conf/nsswitch conventions for Linux apps, and propagate proxy settings and connectivity state to Windows apps via Wine's registry and WinINet.
rationale: Browsers, chat clients, and package managers inside the personalities query network state directly and break without these surfaces.

text: Decision on the authority a terminal session confers on Linux programs it launches (an ambient Linux-personality environment scoped by the terminal's own capabilities) and how a developer escalates or attenuates it.
rationale: Terminals are the one place users expect ambient authority and the policy must be explicit or §9 silently erodes.

text: UPower and logind D-Bus compatibility (battery state, inhibitors, session and seat queries) for Linux apps, backed by the native power and session services.
rationale: Browsers, media players, and desktop environments inside the Linux personality query these interfaces and misbehave without them.

text: Decide which Linux packaging formats the Linux personality supports for end-user installation (Flatpak, AppImage, deb/rpm via distro container, Nix) and which is the recommended first-class path.
rationale: Linux compatibility is a product, and users need a predictable answer to how to install their existing software.

text: Decide whether and how a Linux-personality application may incrementally adopt native interfaces (file chooser, semantic interfaces, capabilities) as an explicit bridge, and what limits keep this from eroding the §3 firewall.
rationale: An all-or-nothing rewrite requirement means no existing application ever becomes native.

text: Publish a five-minute guide and tooling for running an existing Linux application on JakeOS via the personality, as the recommended first developer experience.
rationale: Showing existing software working is the fastest credibility win before anyone writes native code.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the Linux personality implementation depth for each milestone: in-kernel Linux syscall path retained (Phase A), in-kernel translation onto native primitives, or gVisor-style userspace personality, with syscall overhead measured per option.
rationale: Linux compatibility overhead is a tracked 1.0 metric and each option locks in different maintenance and security trade-offs.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Prototype mapping a Linux process to a native Component and its file descriptors to capabilities, and decide whether Linux processes are first-class components or a separate personality-managed construct.
rationale: This determines whether resource domains, tracing and permissions apply uniformly to compatibility software.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide whether the native compositor implements Wayland protocols directly or hosts a nested compatibility compositor, and whether X11 arrives only via Xwayland.
rationale: Linux GUI applications must feel native, and the compositor architecture cannot easily switch later.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide whether xdg-desktop-portal becomes the bridge through which Linux applications reach the native capability-based file chooser, clipboard and screen-share grants.
rationale: Portals are the existing sandbox interface Linux apps already speak, and reusing them avoids inventing a second compatibility permission model.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the level of glibc and systemd emulation the Linux personality provides (real systemd, a systemd-compatible service manager, or none) based on a survey of the top 200 Linux desktop applications' actual dependencies.
rationale: Compatibility is a product, and its scope must be set from evidence about what applications require.

text: Provide a Linux/POSIX compatibility personality that runs existing Linux software.
Linux personality must expose processes to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose PIDs to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose file descriptors to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose POSIX signals to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose /proc to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose /sys to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose BSD sockets to Linux applications.
Linux personality must support fork() for Linux applications.
Linux personality must support exec() for Linux applications.
Linux personality must support epoll for Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose POSIX paths to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose the Linux syscall ABI to Linux applications.
Resolve how a native application explicitly opts into a compatibility environment (capability to a personality, embedded Linux component, or SDK shim) and what authority that grants.
Linux applications execute through a Linux ABI Personality layer.
Phase A: Linux applications must continue functioning normally on the fork; add a regression suite of Linux binaries that must pass on every kernel build.
Phase B: Linux becomes a compatibility personality with its own entry path rather than the default execution model.
Define how the Linux and Windows personalities present native storage objects as POSIX paths and Windows drive letters while respecting capability scope (cross-ref LNX, WIN).
Define how the native dependency model interoperates with Linux personality shared libraries (glibc, distribution libraries) that expect a global /usr/lib namespace (cross-ref LNX).
Define how a user-space native driver coexists with Linux personality expectations (/dev nodes, sysfs, udev events) for the same device (cross-ref LNX).
OCI containers must remain supported for users.
OCI container support belongs to the Linux compatibility personality, never to the native platform.
Integrate an OCI runtime (e.g. runc/crun via podman) inside the Linux personality using personality-provided namespaces, cgroups and overlay filesystem semantics.
Decide which container engine surface to support in the Linux personality (podman, containerd, Docker CLI/socket compatibility) (ADR).
Resolve whether Docker socket API compatibility is required for developer adoption or whether podman-compatible tooling suffices.
Provide a Wayland protocol bridge into the native compositor for Linux GUI applications (§47).
Wayland compatibility may exist for Linux applications, implemented in the Linux personality (§47).
Initially retain the Linux syscall ABI directly in the forked kernel so existing Linux software runs unchanged.
Design the long-term Linux Personality as a layer between Linux ELF binaries and native kernel primitives.
Linux Personality must provide syscall translation onto native primitives.
Linux Personality must provide the POSIX process model (PIDs, parent/child, wait, exit codes).
Linux Personality must provide a file-descriptor namespace over native capabilities.
Linux Personality must provide signals.
Linux Personality must provide /proc.
Linux Personality must provide mounts and a POSIX path namespace synthesised over the native storage model (§25).
Linux Personality must provide Linux security semantics (uid/gid, DAC modes, capabilities(7), seccomp, LSM hooks as needed).
Linux Personality must load Linux ELF binaries including dynamic linking against glibc.
fork() must eventually be implemented as compatibility-layer behaviour over native primitives, never as a native abstraction.
epoll must eventually be implemented as compatibility-layer behaviour over native Operations.
Signal delivery must eventually be implemented over native primitives inside the personality.
pid namespaces must eventually be implemented inside the personality over native Components/ResourceDomains.
Map Linux processes onto Components, TaskGroups and ResourceDomains so Linux software is accounted, inspectable and cancellable like native software.
Resolve how Linux-personality processes acquire capabilities: default compatibility capability profile, path-to-capability mapping, and how the user grants more.
Ensure the Linux personality can host native development environment runtimes and services (§35).
Provide Wayland compatibility for Linux GUI applications.
Provide X11 compatibility where necessary (Xwayland-style server inside the personality).
Provide a D-Bus session and system bus for Linux applications.
Provide desktop portals (xdg-desktop-portal interfaces) backed by native capability choosers.
Provide Linux system conventions: XDG base directories, .desktop entries, icon themes, MIME database.
All Linux GUI compatibility machinery belongs to the Linux personality, not the native platform.
Linux GUI applications must integrate into the native desktop so users do not perceive them as VM applications.
Linux GUI applications must appear as native windows managed by the native compositor.
Linux GUI applications must interoperate with the native clipboard.
Linux GUI applications must interoperate with native drag and drop.
Linux GUI applications must have GPU acceleration (Mesa EGL/Vulkan inside the personality with dma-buf import into the native compositor).
Linux GUI applications must use the native file chooser via portals, receiving capabilities for chosen files (§25).
Linux GUI applications must deliver notifications into the native notification system.
Linux GUI applications must participate in native task switching (launcher, taskbar, alt-tab).
Linux GUI applications must respect native screen scaling including fractional and per-display scaling.
Bridge D-Bus portal requests to native services (file chooser, notifications, screen share, settings).
Evaluate Flatpak and Snap compatibility (runtime, portals, sandbox) and decide whether they run as Linux-personality package sources (ADR).
Linux compatibility must be treated as a product with its own owner, conformance test suite, UX acceptance criteria and release notes — not a syscall shim.

Document the gap between 'running Linux binaries' and 'reproducing a complete Linux environment': inventory the required environment components for each application class (CLI, GUI, games, IDEs, containers).
glibc (and musl) must run unmodified within the Linux personality.
systemd assumptions (sd-bus, socket activation, logind sessions/seats, user units, journald, XDG_RUNTIME_DIR) must be satisfied or emulated for applications that depend on them.
D-Bus system and session buses must be available to Linux applications, with bridges to native services where needed.
procfs (/proc) semantics must be available inside the Linux personality.
sysfs (/sys) semantics must be available inside the Linux personality.
Linux namespaces (pid, mount, net, user, uts, ipc, cgroup) must be available inside the Linux personality for containers and application sandboxes.
Wayland protocol support for Linux GUI applications integrated into the native compositor (cross-ref §47).
X11 support (Xwayland or equivalent) for legacy Linux GUI applications.
PipeWire (and PulseAudio compatibility) for Linux audio and video capture applications.
xdg-desktop-portal implementation bridging Linux portal requests to the native capability-based file chooser, screenshot and notification services.
Linux filesystem conventions (FHS layout, XDG base directories, /tmp, /home, /etc) provided within the personality view without making them the native storage model.
Linux compatibility conformance suite running real applications (Firefox, Chromium, VS Code, Steam, LibreOffice, GIMP, Blender) with tracked pass/fail per release.
Basic Linux compatibility remains intact in V0: an unmodified Linux userspace boots and runs on the fork alongside native components.
Linux GUI compatibility in V0.5 may continue to use existing Linux mechanisms (Wayland/Xwayland, PipeWire) underneath rather than native integration.
Linux compatibility sufficient for developer workflow tools (compilers, build systems, containers, CLI tooling).
Linux applications integrated into the native desktop (taskbar, clipboard, drag/drop, notifications).
Linux compatibility at public-alpha quality against the conformance suite.
Linux personality path: Linux/POSIX ABI implemented over native kernel primitives (cross-ref §46).
